Mining · Ghana

A dated record of what is on your mining lease, and what has changed

Mining leases in Ghana sit alongside farms, towns, rivers and forest reserves, and the ground changes fast. AfriScan maps structures, pits, washing sites, cleared ground and tracks inside your lease and in a ring around it, compares each survey with the last, and gives your land and community teams a ranked list of places that have changed. A person checks the marks before they reach you.

Send your lease boundary See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

A boundary on the cadastre, and ground that will not stay still

“The town is growing into the lease.”

Farms, houses and kiosks move towards lease edges, haul roads and the land you set aside for the next pit. The edge that matters keeps moving, and last year’s walk-over no longer describes it.

“New pits have opened by the river.”

Galamsey pits, washing sites and spoil appear inside and beside leases and along the streams that cross them. Your environment and community teams need to know where the ground and the water have changed, and when.

“We need a record before the renewal.”

A lease renewal, a change of holder or the end of a lease calls for a documented picture of what was on the land, what was built or cleared, and roughly when.

“We have to show reclamation working.”

Reclaimed pits, closed workings and replanted ground need dated evidence of revegetation, set against the ground as it was before.

Who this is for

  • Mine land and property managers
  • Community relations and social performance teams
  • Environment, reclamation and closure managers
  • Mine surveyors and geomatics teams, as users
  • ESIA and RAP consultants
  • Lenders and independent monitors
  • Ghanaian mining service firms

The law in brief

What Act 703 says about land in a mining area

A summary of the public rules as of 27 September 2026, for orientation. It is not legal advice; the sources are linked.

The Minerals and Mining Act 2006 (Act 703) balances the lease holder’s rights against those of the people who own or occupy the land:

  • s.72(3): a lawful occupier keeps grazing and cultivation rights where they do not interfere with mining.
  • s.72(4): in a mining area, the owner or lawful occupier “shall not erect a building or a structure without the consent of the holder of the mining lease”, or of the Minister where consent is unreasonably withheld.
  • s.72(5): the lease holder carries out “a survey of the crops and produce a crop identification map”, in the presence of the occupier and the land-valuation agency.
  • s.72(6): no upgrade “to a higher value crop” without the holder’s written consent.
  • s.73: a compensation claim is copied to the Minister and the valuation agency, the Minister determines it if the parties do not agree, and resettlement is on suitable alternative land at the holder’s cost.

Each of these turns on what stood on the land, and when.

Compensation and the cut-off date

The Minerals and Mining (Compensation and Resettlement) Regulations 2012 (L.I. 2175) fix compensation to a cut-off date published in the district, and the holder “is not liable to pay compensation to any person who undertakes speculative development on land subject to a mineral right after the cut-off date” (reg. 1(8)).

Cut-off-date baselines in Ghana

The law is changing

The Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources reported on 15 July 2026 that Cabinet had endorsed a revised Minerals and Mining Bill, with leases capped at 20 years, district mining committees and mandatory Community Development Agreements (MLNR). L.I. 2462, on mining in forest reserves, has been revoked.

Lease-edge records

What stands inside your lease, and in a ring around it

We list the structures the review confirms inside your lease boundary and in the ring you choose around it, each with an ID, coordinates, its distance to the boundary and the imagery date. Between surveys, new and removed structures, cleared ground and new tracks at the lease edge are flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, so the land team can see where the edge is under pressure. Where you fly drones, a reviewer also checks fence lines and gates, which are too thin to find on satellite imagery.

A reviewer can tag each structure with what the imagery shows, such as main building, outbuilding, livestock enclosure or under construction, which is the starting point for a land-access or resettlement register. Across a whole concession, the same work produces a structure layer your GIS team can load straight into its own system.

We work from the boundary you give us, or from the lease polygon on the Minerals Commission’s public cadastre map, and the report says which one it used.

What you receive

  • A register of structures inside the lease and in the ring around it
  • Change at the lease edge between dated surveys
  • New tracks and access roads into the lease
  • Reviewer categories for each structure, on request
  • A structure layer across the whole concession
  • A PDF report and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

Galamsey and surface excavation

Pits, washing sites and disturbed water on and around your lease

Galamsey leaves marks that imagery can show: pits and trenches, spoil heaps, water-filled excavations and washing sites, cleared ground, new footpaths and tracks, and discoloured water in the streams and rivers downstream. We map them inside your lease and around it, flag new sites between dated surveys, and give your land, environment and community teams a ranked list of places to check.

Detection of pits and spoil is tuned and checked on part of your area before it runs on the rest, and every flagged site is confirmed by a reviewer. Ground-disturbance alerts from Global Forest Watch add a regular screen between surveys; an alert is an indication to check, not proof, and it will not catch every disturbance. When cloud hides the ground, radar comparisons from Copernicus Sentinel-1 data show larger changes, such as clearing and earthworks, even under rainy-season cloud, but not individual small structures, so flagged areas are followed up with optical imagery or drone checks. Drone checks capture more detail, subject to the GCAA authorisations and security clearances each job requires.

Land and water, never people

We describe the ground: where it has been dug, cleared or flooded, when it changed and how large the disturbed area is. We never count, identify or describe the people involved. Underground workings are not visible from above, and a flag is an indication to check, not proof of anything. What you do with the record, and whom you share it with, is your decision.

Forest reserves and river buffers

The edges that environmental permits care about

Many leases border forest reserves or are crossed by rivers. We map where tree cover has been lost or has regrown along a reserve edge, where the ground beside a river has been cleared or dug, and how land cover inside your buffer zones changes between dates, from Copernicus Sentinel data and, where they exist, very-high-resolution scenes. Regular forest-loss alerts from Global Forest Watch are checked by our team before they reach you; they are indications to check, not proof, and will not catch every change.

The Environmental Assessment Regulations 2025 (L.I. 2504) list forest reserves, water bodies and sacred groves among the features a baseline location map must show, so the same layers feed your environmental permit work.

Expansions and resettlement

Record the footprint before the census

When a pit, dump or haul road expands, we produce a dated register of the structures inside the new footprint on the imagery closest to the cut-off date, with reviewer categories and, on request, estimated households with the assumptions stated. After the cut-off date, re-surveys flag new structures in the footprint for your team to check against the census.

The register supports the demographic survey and housing inventory that L.I. 2175 asks a resettlement plan for and, where lenders are involved, the census and asset inventory under IFC Performance Standard 5; it does not replace them. The crop survey and crop identification map under Act 703 s.72(5) stay with you, the occupier and the land-valuation agency, and a dated land-cover layer helps plan them.

Reclamation and closure

Dated evidence that reclaimed land is recovering

Revegetation on reclaimed land

How green cover returns on backfilled pits, closed workings and replanted ground, measured between dates and set against the land before it was disturbed. The record shows direction and extent; closure sign-off and ecological assessment stay with your specialists and the regulator.

Earthworks and volumes

Where the pit is flown by drone, we compare elevation models between visits to show where ground was cut or filled, and calculate stockpile and void volumes for your mine surveyors. The figures support their work; they are not a statutory survey.

The imagery history

What the land looked like before it was disturbed, and when it changed, from archived satellite imagery and open datasets, for renewal, handover and closure files.

Environmental permits

Baseline maps for the Preliminary Environmental Report

Under the Environmental Assessment Regulations 2025 (L.I. 2504), in force since 25 July 2025 under the Environmental Protection Act 2025 (Act 1124), mineral exploration, mining and land reclamation are among the undertakings that need an environmental permit. The Preliminary Environmental Report’s baseline includes “the location map and topographical sheet showing communities, water bodies, forest reserves, sacred groves and other environmentally sensitive areas”, adjacent land use in each direction, and “a concession map is required for a mining undertaking”.

We supply the dated inputs: a land-use and land-cover baseline, the structure register for the concession and the ring around it, and change since earlier imagery. Your environmental consultant prepares and signs the report.

Inputs, not the report

  • Land use and land cover around the concession
  • Structures and settlements, with their distance to the boundary
  • Water bodies and tree cover, and change between dates
  • The imagery named and dated in every layer

Local content

Working through a Ghanaian firm on mine leases

The Minerals Commission’s 6th-edition Local Procurement List, current on 27 September 2026, reserves “Geophysical Ground-based Survey; Mapping, Pitting and Trenching” (item 35) for firms “Strictly Incorporated in Ghana with Exclusive Ghanaian Directors and Shareholders”, requires at least 30 per cent Ghanaian directors and shareholders for airborne survey (item 36), and reserves security services to Ghanaians (item 20).

So on a mining lease, AfriScan works as the technology supplier to a qualifying Ghanaian firm, which holds the contract with the lease holder, and our work is described as land and environmental mapping, never as security. Whether remote satellite analysis falls under item 35 is a question for counsel; the proposal sets out the arrangement for your contract.

Your own drone imagery

If your survey team already flies the lease, send the orthophotos or GeoTIFFs. We run the same structure, excavation and change analysis on them, with a reviewer confirming each result, and use satellite scenes between flights. Results depend on the imagery’s resolution and quality, which we check on a sample first.

Working with AfriScan in Ghana

How it works

From lease boundary to reviewed record

  1. Scope

    You send the lease boundary and the ring to cover, and tell us what the record is for. We agree the dates, imagery and deliverables in a written proposal, with the Ghanaian firm that will hold the contract.

  2. Screen

    Dated satellite scenes, open building datasets and your own drone imagery give the first register of structures, excavations and cleared ground.

  3. Review

    A person confirms, corrects and adds to what the models propose, and lists what the imagery cannot settle for a ground check.

  4. Deliver and repeat

    The report and GIS layers go to the contacts you name, and re-surveys follow the schedule you set, with a notice of what changed and where.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map structures, pits, washing sites, cleared ground and tracks visible from the air
  • Flag change at the lease edge and around it between dated surveys
  • Record the footprint on the cut-off date, and what appeared after it
  • Track revegetation on reclaimed land

What we don’t do

  • Identify, count or follow people, or provide security or enforcement
  • See underground workings, or verify title and tenure
  • Produce the crop identification map or cadastral plans
  • Decide whether a structure or working is authorised

Frequently asked questions

Do you supply security or enforcement services?

No. We map land and assets for the lease holder. The register shows what is on the ground and when it changed; decisions about the land stay with you and the authorities. We do not identify, count or follow people, and our work is not a security service.

Can you map galamsey pits and washing sites on our lease?

Yes, where they are visible from above. Pits, spoil heaps, water-filled excavations and washing sites, cleared ground and discoloured water in streams and rivers are mapped from dated imagery, and new sites are flagged between surveys and confirmed by a reviewer. Detection is tuned and checked on part of your area before it runs on the rest. Underground workings, shafts under cover and sites hidden by canopy or cloud are not visible.

Which lease boundary do you use?

The one you give us, or the lease polygon from the Minerals Commission’s public cadastre map if you ask us to use it. The report says whose boundary it used. We do not verify title, tenure or surface rights, and a boundary that needs surveying or beaconing is work for a professional land surveyor.

Does your record show that a building went up without our consent?

It shows what stood where on each imagery date, and the first date on which a structure appears. Under Act 703 s.72(4), building in a mining area needs the lease holder’s consent, or the Minister’s where consent is unreasonably withheld. Whether consent was given, and what follows, is for you, the Minister and the courts; the record supports those processes.

Can you produce the crop identification map?

No. Act 703 s.72(5) asks the lease holder to survey the crops and produce the crop identification map in the presence of the occupier and the land-valuation agency. We can supply a dated land-cover layer, showing cropland, tree cover and built-up land, to help plan that survey.

How do you work with local-content rules on a mine?

Item 35 of the Minerals Commission’s list, “Geophysical Ground-based Survey; Mapping, Pitting and Trenching”, is reserved to firms incorporated in Ghana with exclusively Ghanaian directors and shareholders. Whether it reaches remote satellite analysis is a question for counsel, so on a mining lease AfriScan works as the technology supplier to a qualifying Ghanaian firm, which holds the contract with you. Tell us if you already work with one.

Send your lease boundary

Send the lease or concession boundary (Shapefile, GeoPackage, KML or GeoJSON), the ring you want around it, the dates the record should cover and what it is for: an expansion, a renewal, a cut-off date or reclamation. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
